stem:
What does an in-order traversal of this binary search tree visit?

```
        8
       / \
      3   10
     / \    \
    1   6    14
       / \   /
      4   7 13
```

options.why: That is pre-order: the root is visited before its subtrees.
In-order visits left subtree, node, right subtree, which for a BST is ascending order.
That is post-order: each node is visited after both of its subtrees.
That is level-order (breadth-first), visiting the tree one depth at a time.

explanation: In-order traversal is left, node, right. The BST property puts every smaller key in the left subtree and every larger key in the right, so an in-order walk of any valid BST produces its keys in sorted order. That property is also the basis of many BST checks and of "kth smallest" queries.

stem: Every complete binary tree is also a full binary tree.

options.text: True
options.why: A complete tree may have one node on its last internal level with only a left child, which a full tree forbids.

options.text: False
options.why: Complete only requires levels filled left to right; full requires every node to have 0 or 2 children.

explanation: A complete binary tree fills every level except possibly the last, and fills the last level from the left. A full binary tree requires every node to have zero or two children. A complete tree with 2 nodes (a root with one left child) is complete but not full. A perfect tree is both full and complete.
reference: NIST DADS: complete binary tree; full binary tree

stem: Match each kind of binary tree with its definition.

options.text: Every node has either 0 or 2 children
Every level is filled except possibly the last, which is filled from the left
All internal nodes have 2 children and all leaves are at the same depth
Every parent has exactly one child, so the tree is a chain

explanation: These shapes matter for complexity. A perfect tree of height h has 2^(h+1) − 1 nodes. A complete tree is what an array-backed heap uses. A degenerate tree behaves like a linked list, which turns O(log n) BST operations into O(n).

stem: Which auxiliary data structure does a standard level-order (breadth-first) traversal of a binary tree use?

options.text: A stack, pushing the right child before the left one
options.why: Pushing right before left on a stack gives an iterative pre-order traversal, not level order.

options.text: A FIFO queue of the nodes waiting to be visited
options.why: A queue releases nodes in the order they were discovered, which is one depth level after another.

options.text: A min-heap keyed by each node's value
options.why: A heap would visit nodes in value order, which is unrelated to their depth in the tree.

options.text: No extra structure; recursion alone is enough
options.why: Plain recursion follows depth-first order; level order needs to remember a whole frontier.

explanation: Breadth-first traversal enqueues the root, then repeatedly dequeues a node, visits it, and enqueues its children. Because a queue is first-in first-out, all nodes at depth d come out before any node at depth d + 1. Processing the queue in batches of its current length lets you separate the levels.

stem: Height is counted in edges, so a single node has height 0. What is the maximum number of nodes in a binary tree of height 3? Type a number.
explanation: Level d holds at most 2^d nodes, so a tree of height h holds at most 2^0 + 2^1 + … + 2^h = 2^(h+1) − 1 nodes. For h = 3 that is 2^4 − 1 = 15, which is a perfect binary tree. If height counted nodes instead of edges, the formula would be 2^h − 1.

stem: A trie stores 100,000 English words. What is the time complexity of checking whether any stored word starts with a prefix of length m?

options.text: O(log n), because the trie keeps its words sorted
options.why: A trie isn't searched by comparing whole words, so its cost doesn't depend on the number of words.

options.text: O(m), following one child link per prefix character
options.why: Follow one child pointer per character of the prefix; the walk is independent of the word count.

options.text: O(n · m), checking every stored word against the prefix
options.why: That is the brute-force scan the trie exists to avoid.

options.text: O(1), the same as membership in a hash set
options.why: A hash set gives O(1) average lookups for exact words but can't answer prefix queries directly.

explanation: Each trie node branches on the next character, so `startsWith(prefix)` walks at most m edges and either falls off (no match) or ends on a node, in which case some word has that prefix. A hash set of words can only answer prefix questions by hashing every prefix in advance or scanning all words.
reference: Sedgewick & Wayne, Algorithms 4th ed., Section 5.2: Tries

stem:
Put the nodes of this tree in the order a post-order traversal visits them.

```
      A
     / \
    B   C
   / \
  D   E
```

options.text: A
B
C
D
E

explanation: Post-order visits the left subtree, then the right subtree, then the node itself. The left subtree of A gives D, E, then B. The right subtree gives C. The root A comes last, which is why post-order suits work that needs children finished first, such as freeing memory or computing subtree heights.

stem: Which two statements about plain (unbalanced) binary search trees are true? (Choose two.)

options.text: Inserting keys in sorted order produces a chain with height n − 1
options.why: Each new key is larger than everything before it, so it always goes to the right.

options.text: Search takes O(n) in the worst case
options.why: On a chain, a search may have to walk every node.

options.text: Search always takes O(log n) whatever the insertion order
options.why: Only balanced trees guarantee O(log n); a plain BST depends on insertion order.

options.text: An in-order traversal lists the keys in descending order
options.why: In-order lists them in ascending order, because smaller keys are on the left.

options.text: Every BST is height-balanced as long as its keys are distinct
options.why: Distinct keys can still be inserted in an order that makes the tree arbitrarily skewed.

explanation: A BST's height depends on insertion order. Sorted input creates a degenerate tree that behaves like a linked list, so search, insert and delete degrade to O(n). Self-balancing trees (AVL, red-black) and random insertion orders keep the height logarithmic.

stem:
What is the post-order traversal of this tree?

```
        8
       / \
      3   10
     / \    \
    1   6    14
       / \   /
      4   7 13
```

options.why: This visits 14 before its left child 13; post-order must finish 13 first.
Left subtree (1 4 7 6 3), then right subtree (13 14 10), then the root 8.
This puts 1 after 6, but 1 is the left child of 3 and comes first.
This mixes in-order for the left subtree with post-order for the right.

explanation: Post-order is left, right, node. The left subtree rooted at 3 yields 1, then 6's subtree (4, 7, 6), then 3. The right subtree rooted at 10 has only a right child 14, whose left child 13 comes before 14, then 10. The root 8 is last.

stem:
What does a level-order traversal of this tree visit?

```
        8
       / \
      3   10
     / \    \
    1   6    14
       / \   /
      4   7 13
```

options.why: This finishes 3's whole subtree before 14, which is depth-first behaviour.
This visits each level right to left; standard level order goes left to right.
Depth 0: 8; depth 1: 3, 10; depth 2: 1, 6, 14; depth 3: 4, 7, 13.
That is pre-order, which goes deep before it goes wide.

explanation: Level order visits nodes by depth, left to right within a depth. A queue produces exactly this order: 8, then its children 3 and 10, then 1, 6 (children of 3) and 14 (child of 10), then 4, 7 and 13.

stem:
You delete key 3 from this BST using the in-order successor strategy for a node with two children. Which key takes 3's place?

```
        8
       / \
      3   10
     / \    \
    1   6    14
       / \   /
      4   7 13
```

options.text: 1, the left child of the deleted node
options.why: Promoting the left child would put 6's subtree, with its larger keys, in the wrong place.
The successor is the smallest key in 3's right subtree: go right to 6, then left as far as possible.

options.text: 6, the right child of the deleted node
options.why: 6 has a left child (4) smaller than it, so 6 is not the smallest key in that subtree.

options.text: 7, the largest key in the right subtree
options.why: The largest key would break the ordering with the other keys still in that subtree.

explanation: To delete a node with two children, copy its in-order successor (the minimum of its right subtree) into it, then delete the successor, which has no left child. Here the successor of 3 is 4, so 3 becomes 4 and the old 4 node is removed. Using the in-order predecessor (the maximum of the left subtree, here 1) is the symmetric, equally valid strategy.

stem:
What does `kth_smallest(root, 4)` return for this BST?

```
        8
       / \
      3   10
     / \    \
    1   6    14
       / \   /
      4   7 13
```

```python
def kth_smallest(root, k):
    stack, node = [], root
    while stack or node:
        while node:
            stack.append(node)
            node = node.left
        node = stack.pop()
        k -= 1
        if k == 0:
            return node.val
        node = node.right
```

options.text: `4`, the third key visited plus one
options.why: Counting starts at 1: the visits go 1, 3, 4, 6, so 4 is only the third.

options.text: `7`, because the walk counts from the root
options.why: The loop counts in-order visits, starting from the smallest key, not from the root.

options.text: `8`, the root, reached after four pushes
options.why: Pushes don't count; k only drops when a node is popped and visited.
The iterative in-order walk visits 1, 3, 4, 6 and stops on the fourth key.

explanation: This is an iterative in-order traversal that stops early. It pushes the left spine, pops the smallest remaining node, counts it, then moves to its right subtree. The visit order is 1, 3, 4, 6, …, so the fourth smallest key is 6. It runs in O(h + k) time rather than visiting the whole tree.

stem:
What is the lowest common ancestor of 4 and 13 in this BST?

```
        8
       / \
      3   10
     / \    \
    1   6    14
       / \   /
      4   7 13
```

options.why: 4 is smaller than 8 and 13 is larger, so the paths split at the root.
3 is an ancestor of 4 but not of 13, which lies in the root's right subtree.
10 is an ancestor of 13 but not of 4.
6 is 4's parent, but 13 is nowhere in 6's subtree.

explanation: In a BST you can find the LCA by walking from the root: if both keys are smaller, go left; if both are larger, go right; otherwise the current node is where their paths diverge. At the root 8, 4 < 8 < 13, so 8 is the LCA. For 4 and 7 the walk would go left to 3, then right to 6.

stem: Height is counted in edges. What is the minimum possible height of a binary tree with 100 nodes? Type a number.
explanation: A tree of height h holds at most 2^(h+1) − 1 nodes. Height 5 allows only 63 nodes, while height 6 allows 127, so 100 nodes need height at least 6. In general the minimum height is ⌊log₂ n⌋, and ⌊log₂ 100⌋ = 6.

stem: A search box must suggest every stored product name that begins with what the user has typed so far, updating on each keystroke. Which structure fits best?

options.text: A hash set of all names, checked once per keystroke
options.why: A hash set answers exact matches only, so you would scan every name per keystroke.

options.text: An unsorted list scanned with `startswith` on every keystroke
options.why: That costs O(n · m) per keystroke, which won't scale to large catalogues.

options.text: A trie, walking down one node for each typed character
options.why: The walk reaches the prefix node in O(m), and its subtree holds exactly the matching names.

options.text: A max-heap keyed by the length of each product name
options.why: A heap orders by one priority and can't group names by their prefix.

explanation: A trie groups words by shared prefixes. After the user types m characters you are at one node, and every word in its subtree is a match. Each new keystroke moves one level deeper. Production autocomplete adds ranking, for example storing the top-k suggestions at each node, but the prefix lookup itself is O(m).
reference: Sedgewick & Wayne, Algorithms 4th ed., Section 5.2: Tries

stem: Which traversals can be implemented iteratively using a single explicit stack and no parent pointers? (Choose three.)

options.text: Pre-order
options.why: Pop a node, visit it, then push its right child before its left child.

options.text: In-order
options.why: Push the left spine, pop and visit, then move to the popped node's right child.

options.text: Post-order
options.why: Track the last visited node, or reverse a modified pre-order, to visit children first.

options.text: Level-order
options.why: Level order needs first-in first-out behaviour; a stack produces depth-first order.

options.text: None of them, because recursion is required for tree traversals
options.why: Any recursive traversal can be rewritten with an explicit stack that replaces the call stack.

explanation: The three depth-first traversals all replace the call stack with an explicit one. Post-order is the fiddliest: either remember the previously visited node so you know when both children are done, or produce node-right-left with a stack and reverse it. Level order needs a queue.

stem: Given only the pre-order and post-order traversals of a binary tree with distinct values, the tree is always uniquely determined.

options.text: True
options.why: A root A with only a left child B and a root A with only a right child B share both traversals.

options.text: False
options.why: Without in-order you can't tell whether a single child is a left or a right child.

explanation: Both trees give pre-order A, B and post-order B, A, so the pair is ambiguous whenever a node has exactly one child. Pre-order plus in-order (or post-order plus in-order) is unique for distinct values, because in-order tells you where the root splits left from right. Pre-order plus post-order is unique only for full binary trees.
reference: GeeksforGeeks: Construct a full binary tree from preorder and postorder

stem:
What does `depth(root)` return for this tree?

```
        8
       / \
      3   10
     / \    \
    1   6    14
       / \   /
      4   7 13
```

```python
def depth(node):
    if node is None:
        return 0
    return 1 + max(depth(node.left), depth(node.right))
```

options.text: `3`, the height measured in edges
options.why: This function returns 0 for an empty tree and 1 for a single node, so it counts nodes.
The longest root-to-leaf path is 8-3-6-4 (or 8-10-14-13), which has four nodes.

options.text: `9`, the total number of nodes in the tree
options.why: Counting nodes would add the two subtree results instead of taking their maximum.

options.text: `5`, counting the empty child below each leaf
options.why: The None check returns 0, so empty children add nothing to the count.

explanation: This definition counts nodes on the longest root-to-leaf path. The path 8 → 3 → 6 → 4 has four nodes, so the result is 4, which is a height of 3 in edges. Interview problems such as LeetCode's "maximum depth" use this node-counting convention, so state which one you mean.
reference: LeetCode 104: Maximum Depth of Binary Tree

stem: Match each requirement with the tree-based structure that fits it best.

options.text: Trie
Segment tree
B+ tree
AVL tree

prompts.text: Suggest every word that starts with the letters typed so far
Answer "minimum value in positions i..j" while single positions keep changing
Index a disk-resident table so range scans read few pages
An in-memory ordered map with strict height balance for fast lookups

explanation: A trie organises keys by prefix. A segment tree stores aggregates for ranges, giving O(log n) range queries and point updates. A B+ tree has a high fan-out and linked leaves, which suits disk pages and range scans in databases. An AVL tree is a binary search tree that rebalances to keep its height under about 1.44 log₂ n.

stem:
What does `is_bst(root)` return for this tree?

```
      5
     / \
    3   8
     \
      7
```

```python
def is_bst(node):
    if node is None:
        return True
    if node.left and node.left.val >= node.val:
        return False
    if node.right and node.right.val <= node.val:
        return False
    return is_bst(node.left) and is_bst(node.right)
```

options.text: `True`, although the tree is not a valid BST
options.why: Each node is only compared with its direct children, so 7 sitting under 5's left subtree goes unnoticed.

options.text: `False`, because 7 is larger than the root 5
options.why: The function never compares 7 with 5; it only compares 7 with its parent 3.

options.text: `False`, because 3 has a right child but no left child
options.why: Missing children are allowed; the checks skip them.

options.text: `True`, and the tree is a valid BST
options.why: Every key in 5's left subtree must be less than 5, and 7 is not.

explanation: The BST property is about whole subtrees, not just parent and child. 7 > 3 satisfies the local check at node 3, but 7 sits in the left subtree of 5, which requires every key to be below 5. This local-check bug is one of the most common interview mistakes. Fix it by passing the allowed (low, high) range down the recursion.

options.text: Also compare each node with its grandparent before recursing
options.why: Violations can come from any ancestor, not only the grandparent, so this still misses cases.

options.text: Swap the order of the two recursive calls so the right subtree is checked first
options.why: The order of the calls doesn't matter; the missing information is the ancestors' bounds.

options.text: Use `>` and `<` instead of `>=` and `<=` in the comparisons
options.why: That only changes how equal keys are treated and still checks just direct children.

options.text: Pass (low, high) bounds down the recursion and require low < val < high
options.why: Each node must lie strictly within the range set by all its ancestors.

explanation: Carry an open interval: the root may be anything, a left child must be below its parent and above whatever lower bound the parent had, and so on. `valid(n, lo, hi)` checks `lo < n.val < hi` and recurses with `(lo, n.val)` and `(n.val, hi)`. An equivalent approach is an in-order traversal that checks each key exceeds the previous one. Both run in O(n).

stem:
The diameter of a binary tree is the number of edges on its longest path between any two nodes. A candidate computes it as `height(root.left) + height(root.right)`, where `height` counts nodes. What does that return for this tree, and what is the true diameter?

```
          1
         /
        2
       / \
      3   6
     /     \
    4       7
   /         \
  5           8
```

options.text: Returns 6; the true diameter is also 6
options.why: At the root the right subtree is empty, so the formula only sees the left side.

options.text: Returns 4; the true diameter is 7
options.why: The longest path 5-4-3-2-6-7-8 has 7 nodes but only 6 edges.

options.text: Returns 4; the true diameter is 6
options.why: The longest path, 5 to 8, bends at node 2, not at the root.

options.text: Returns 5; the true diameter is 6
options.why: height(2) counts 4 nodes and the empty right subtree counts 0, giving 4.

explanation: The longest path need not pass through the root. Here it runs 5-4-3-2-6-7-8 and turns at node 2, for 6 edges. The correct algorithm computes, at every node, left height + right height, and keeps the maximum seen, all in one O(n) post-order pass. Checking only the root gives 4 + 0 = 4.

options.text: O(n), because each node is visited once by `is_balanced`
options.why: Each visit also calls `height`, which walks the whole subtree below that node.

options.text: O(n log n), because the heights shrink by half at each level
options.why: Halving only happens in balanced trees; on a chain each subtree is one node smaller.

options.text: O(1), because the check fails at the root right away
options.why: The recursive calls run first, so nothing short-circuits before the heights are computed.

options.text: O(n²), as each shorter suffix chain's height is recomputed
options.why: The heights of subtrees of sizes n−1, n−2, … are all computed: about n²/2 steps.

explanation: Every node calls `height` on its children, and on a chain those subtrees have sizes n−1, n−2, …, 1, so the total work is about n²/2. In practice, doubling n from 400 to 800 quadrupled the `height` calls (160,400 to 640,800). The O(n) fix computes height and balance in one post-order pass, returning −1 as soon as any subtree is unbalanced.

stem: Put the steps of inserting a key into an AVL tree in order.

options.text: Insert the key as a new leaf, exactly as in a plain BST
Update heights on the path back up towards the root
Find the lowest ancestor whose balance factor is now +2 or −2
Classify the imbalance as LL, LR, RR or RL from the path taken
Apply the matching single or double rotation at that ancestor

explanation: AVL insertion is a BST insert followed by repair on the way back up. The first unbalanced ancestor is fixed with one rotation (LL, RR) or two (LR, RL), and after an insertion that single fix restores the original height of that subtree, so no ancestor above it needs another rotation. Deletion is different: it may need rotations at several ancestors.
reference: Weiss, Data Structures and Algorithm Analysis, Section 4.4: AVL trees

stem: You insert 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 25 in that order into an empty AVL tree. Which key is the root at the end?

options.text: 20, which became the root after inserting 30
options.why: 20 was the root for a while, but inserting 25 triggers a right-left rotation at 20.
Inserting 25 unbalances 20 (RL case); the double rotation lifts 30 to the root.

options.text: 10, the first key inserted
options.why: Inserting 30 already forced a left rotation at 10.

options.text: 25, the last key inserted
options.why: New keys start as leaves; 25 ends up as a leaf under 20.

explanation: After 10, 20, 30 a left rotation makes 20 the root. Inserting 40 and 50 unbalances 30, and a left rotation there gives 20(10, 40(30, 50)). Inserting 25 goes into 30's left subtree, so 20 has balance −2 with a right-left shape. A right rotation at 40 then a left rotation at 20 make 30 the root, with 20(10, 25) on the left and 40(50) on the right. The level order is 30, 20, 40, 10, 25, 50.
reference: Weiss, Data Structures and Algorithm Analysis, Section 4.4: AVL trees

stem: You insert 30, then 10, then 20 into an empty AVL tree. Which rotations restore balance?

options.text: A single right rotation at 30, making 10 the new root
options.why: A single right rotation suits the left-left case; here 20 is a left-right grandchild.

options.text: A single left rotation at 10, leaving 30 as the root
options.why: That fixes the shape below 30 but leaves 30 unbalanced.

options.text: A left rotation at 10, then a right rotation at 30
options.why: The left-right case needs a double rotation that makes 20 the root.

options.text: No rotation, because 20 lies between 10 and 30
options.why: The node 30 has balance +2 after the insert, which AVL never allows.

explanation: After inserting, 30 has a left child 10 whose right child is 20: a left-right (LR) imbalance. Rotating left at 10 turns it into a left-left shape (30 → 20 → 10), and rotating right at 30 finishes the job, giving 20 at the root with children 10 and 30. A single right rotation at 30 would make 10 the root with 20 still in the wrong place.
reference: Weiss, Data Structures and Algorithm Analysis, Section 4.4: AVL trees

stem: Why do relational databases index tables with B+ trees rather than binary search trees? (Choose two.)

options.text: High fan-out keeps the tree only a few levels deep, so lookups read few disk pages
options.why: Each node fills a page with hundreds of keys, so a billion rows need about 4 levels.

options.text: Leaves are linked in key order, so range scans walk leaf to leaf
options.why: After finding the start of a range, the scan never climbs back through the tree.

options.text: B+ trees give O(1) lookups, while BSTs give O(log n)
options.why: B+ tree lookups are still logarithmic, just with a very large base.

options.text: B+ trees never need to split or merge nodes after inserts
options.why: Inserts split full nodes and deletes may merge them; that is how they stay balanced.

options.text: B+ trees keep all keys in the root node
options.why: Keys are spread over many nodes; only separator keys live in the internal levels.

explanation: Disk and SSD reads happen in pages, so a structure that packs many keys per node minimises I/O. With a fan-out of a few hundred, three or four levels cover billions of rows, and the upper levels usually stay cached in memory. B+ trees keep all records (or row pointers) in the leaves and chain the leaves, which makes `BETWEEN` and `ORDER BY` scans sequential.
reference: CLRS, Chapter 18: B-Trees; PostgreSQL docs: B-Tree Indexes

stem: In a Fenwick tree (binary indexed tree), `i & -i` gives the size of the range that index i covers. What is `12 & -12`? Type a number.
explanation: 12 is 1100 in binary, and −12 in two's complement keeps only its lowest set bit in common, so `12 & -12` = 100 = 4. Fenwick index 12 therefore stores the sum of positions 9 to 12. A prefix query repeatedly subtracts this lowest bit (12 → 8 → 0), and an update repeatedly adds it, so both take O(log n).
reference: Fenwick, "A New Data Structure for Cumulative Frequency Tables" (1994)

stem: An array of n numbers needs "sum of positions i..j" queries interleaved with single-position updates. With a segment tree, what are the build, query and update costs?

options.text: Build O(n log n), query O(log n), update O(1)
options.why: An update must refresh every ancestor of the changed leaf, which is O(log n) nodes.

options.text: Build O(n), query O(1), update O(n)
options.why: O(1) queries with O(n) updates describe a plain prefix-sum array.

options.text: Build O(n), query O(log n), update O(log n)
options.why: Building fills about 2n nodes bottom-up; each query and update touches O(log n) nodes.

options.text: Build O(n), query O(√n), update O(1)
options.why: That trade-off belongs to square-root decomposition, not to a segment tree.

explanation: A segment tree stores an aggregate for each range in a balanced binary tree over the array. Building computes every internal node once from its children, so it is O(n). A range query splits into O(log n) stored ranges, and a point update recomputes the O(log n) ancestors of one leaf. A prefix-sum array gives O(1) queries but O(n) updates.

stem: A binary tree with distinct values has pre-order `[3, 9, 20, 15, 7]` and in-order `[9, 3, 15, 20, 7]`. What is its post-order traversal?

options.why: This puts 20 before its right child 7; post-order visits both children of 20 first.
The root 3 has left child 9 and right child 20, which has children 15 and 7.
This visits the right subtree before the left one; post-order goes left first.
In-order shows 15 left of 20 and 7 right of it, so 15 comes first.

explanation: Pre-order's first value, 3, is the root. In in-order, 9 sits left of 3 and 15, 20, 7 sit right of it. In the right part, pre-order lists 20 first, so 20 is that subtree's root, with 15 to its left and 7 to its right. Post-order is then left (9), right subtree (15, 7, 20), root (3).
reference: LeetCode 105: Construct Binary Tree from Preorder and Inorder Traversal

stem:
What is the right-side view of this tree, meaning the last node of each level when the tree is seen from the right?

```
        8
       / \
      3   10
     / \    \
    1   6    14
       / \   /
      4   7 13
```

options.why: The deepest level also counts; its only visible node is 13.
7 is the rightmost node in 3's subtree, but 13 is further right on that level.
This mixes nodes from the left subtree with the true rightmost nodes; take the last node of each level.
Levels are [8], [3, 10], [1, 6, 14] and [4, 7, 13]; take the last of each.

explanation: The right-side view is the last node in each level of a level-order traversal, not the right spine. 13 is a left child, but it is the rightmost node at depth 3, so it is visible. Process the queue level by level and record the final node of each batch; that runs in O(n).
reference: LeetCode 199: Binary Tree Right Side View

stem: You serialise a binary tree (not a BST) by writing its pre-order values, without markers for missing children, so a root 1 with a single child 2 becomes "1,2". Why can't you rebuild the original tree from that string?

options.text: Pre-order loses the root, which is only recorded by post-order
options.why: Pre-order always starts with the root, so the root is never lost.

options.text: Pre-order output depends on node values, so duplicates corrupt it
options.why: This fails even when every value is distinct.

options.text: Without null markers you can't tell if 2 was a left or right child
options.why: Adding a marker such as "#" for every missing child makes pre-order unambiguous.

options.text: The string is too short; you would also need the height of every node
options.why: Heights aren't needed once each missing child is recorded.

explanation: Plain pre-order loses the tree's shape: "1,2" fits both 1 with a left child 2 and 1 with a right child 2. Writing a sentinel for every empty child, for example "1,2,#,#,#" against "1,#,2,#,#", lets a recursive reader rebuild the exact shape in O(n). A BST is different: plain pre-order is enough there, because the ordering decides where each key goes.
reference: LeetCode 297: Serialize and Deserialize Binary Tree

stem: You need the lowest common ancestor of two nodes p and q in a general binary tree (not a BST) without parent pointers. Which two statements are true? (Choose two.)

options.text: The node where p and q are found in different subtrees is the LCA
options.why: Or a node that is itself p or q with the other one below it.

options.text: The BST shortcut of comparing values to choose a side doesn't apply
options.why: Values in a general binary tree have no order to steer the search.

options.text: The LCA can't be found without parent pointers
options.why: A single recursive post-order pass finds it with only child pointers.

options.text: The search takes O(log n) time even on a skewed tree
options.why: Without ordering you may need to visit every node, which is O(n).

options.text: It is always the parent of whichever of p and q is deeper
options.why: That only holds when the two nodes happen to be siblings.

explanation: The standard solution recurses: if the current node is p or q, return it. Otherwise recurse into both children, and if both sides return something, the current node is the LCA; if only one does, pass that result up. This visits each node once, O(n) time and O(h) stack. In a BST you can instead steer by value in O(h).
reference: LeetCode 236: Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Tree

stem: Morris in-order traversal visits every node of a binary tree without a stack or recursion. How does it achieve O(1) extra space?

options.text: It stores each node's visited flag in a spare bit of the node's value field
options.why: It doesn't mark nodes; it uses the null right pointers of in-order predecessors.

options.text: It reuses predecessors' null right pointers as temporary return links
options.why: These threads let it climb back up without a stack, and the tree is restored afterwards.

options.text: It visits nodes in level order, needing only a few pointers
options.why: Level order needs a queue that can hold a whole level of the tree.

options.text: It sorts the node values first and then reads them back in ascending order
options.why: Sorting needs extra space and isn't a traversal of the tree's shape.

explanation: For each node with a left subtree, Morris finds the in-order predecessor (the rightmost node of the left subtree). The first time, it points the predecessor's right pointer back at the current node and goes left. The second time it reaches that thread, it removes it, visits the node and goes right. Each edge is walked a constant number of times, so time is O(n) and extra space O(1). The tree is modified during the walk, so it isn't safe while other threads read it.
reference: Morris, "Traversing binary trees simply and cheaply" (1979)

stem: How many structurally different binary search trees can hold the keys 1, 2, 3 and 4? Type a number.
explanation: The count is the Catalan number C₄. Choosing root k leaves k − 1 keys on the left and 4 − k on the right, so C₄ = C₀C₃ + C₁C₂ + C₂C₁ + C₃C₀ = 5 + 2 + 2 + 5 = 14. The closed form is C(2n, n) / (n + 1) = 70 / 5 = 14.

stem: Height is counted in edges, so a single node has height 0. What is the minimum number of nodes an AVL tree of height 4 can have?

options.text: 9, one more node than a height-3 tree needs
options.why: Each extra level needs a whole minimal subtree of the level below, not one node.

options.text: 16, the size of a perfect tree with that many leaves
options.why: AVL trees may be sparser than perfect trees; that is what the bound measures.
N(h) = N(h−1) + N(h−2) + 1 gives 1, 2, 4, 7, 12 for heights 0 to 4.

options.text: 5, a single path from the root down to a leaf
options.why: A path of 5 nodes violates the AVL rule at every node with only one child.

explanation: The sparsest AVL tree of height h has a root, one subtree of height h−1 and one of height h−2, each as sparse as possible. So N(h) = N(h−1) + N(h−2) + 1, which grows like the Fibonacci numbers. From N(0) = 1 and N(1) = 2 you get 4, 7, 12. That Fibonacci growth is why AVL height is at most about 1.44 log₂ n.
reference: Weiss, Data Structures and Algorithm Analysis, Section 4.4: AVL trees

stem:
What is the zigzag level-order traversal of this tree? Level 0 reads left to right, level 1 right to left, and so on.

```
        8
       / \
      3   10
     / \    \
    1   6    14
       / \   /
      4   7 13
```

options.why: The last level is odd-numbered (level 3), so it must be read right to left.
Levels 1 and 3 are reversed; levels 0 and 2 keep their natural order.
This reverses the even levels instead; level 1 must already read right to left.
Level 2 is even-numbered, so it keeps left-to-right order.

explanation: Do a normal level-order traversal, then reverse every odd-numbered level, or fill each level from the appropriate end of a deque. The levels left to right are [8], [3, 10], [1, 6, 14] and [4, 7, 13]. Reversing levels 1 and 3 gives [[8], [10, 3], [1, 6, 14], [13, 7, 4]].
reference: LeetCode 103: Binary Tree Zigzag Level Order Traversal

options.why: The function stops at the root, because its value 1 already equals the target.

options.text: Returns `True`; the correct answer is `True`
options.why: The only root-to-leaf path is 1 → 2, which sums to 3, not 1.

options.text: Returns `True`; the correct answer is `False`
options.why: It accepts a path ending at the root, which isn't a leaf.

options.text: Returns `False`; the correct answer is `True`
options.why: The function matches at the root, and no path sums to 1.

explanation: A root-to-leaf path must end at a node with no children. The bug checks the remaining target at every node, so it accepts partial paths. The fix checks `node.val == target` only when the node is a leaf. With that fix, target 1 gives False and target 3 gives True.

stem: Which three of these are invariants of a red-black tree? (Choose three.)

options.text: The root is black
options.why: Recolouring the root black is always safe and simplifies the other rules.

options.text: A red node never has a red child
options.why: Together with equal black heights, this bounds the longest path at twice the shortest.

options.text: Every path from a node down to a null leaf passes the same number of black nodes
options.why: This equal black height is what keeps the tree balanced overall.

options.text: The left and right subtree heights of every node differ by at most 1
options.why: That is the AVL rule; red-black trees allow more imbalance.

options.text: The tree's height is at most log₂(n + 1)
options.why: The guaranteed bound is 2·log₂(n + 1), twice that.

explanation: The red-black rules are: every node is red or black, the root is black, null leaves count as black, red nodes have black children, and all root-to-null paths have the same black count. They imply height ≤ 2·log₂(n + 1). This is looser than AVL's bound of about 1.44·log₂ n, but it needs fewer rotations: at most two per insertion and three per deletion.

stem: Standard libraries such as Java's `TreeMap` and many C++ `std::map` implementations use red-black trees rather than AVL trees. What is the usual reason?

options.text: Red-black trees have strictly shorter heights, so lookups are always faster
options.why: AVL trees are more tightly balanced, so their lookups are usually slightly faster.

options.text: They do fewer rotations on insert and delete, which suits mixed workloads
options.why: Looser balance means at most 2 rotations per insert and 3 per delete.

options.text: Red-black trees don't need any rebalancing after a deletion
options.why: They do rebalance after deletions, with recolouring and up to three rotations.

options.text: AVL trees can't store duplicate keys, which a map needs
options.why: Duplicate handling is a policy choice, and maps don't store duplicate keys anyway.

explanation: Both give O(log n) operations. AVL keeps a tighter bound (about 1.44 log₂ n against 2 log₂ n), which favours read-heavy workloads, but it may rotate at many ancestors after a deletion. Red-black trees accept slightly taller trees in exchange for cheaper, bounded restructuring on updates, which suits general-purpose maps.

stem: A genome text of length n is fixed, and you must answer many queries of the form "where does pattern P (length m) occur?". Which preprocessing structure gives fast queries without rescanning the text each time?

options.text: A trie of all distinct words in the text, split on spaces
options.why: Patterns can start mid-word or span any characters, so a word trie misses them.

options.text: A balanced BST of the text's characters keyed by position
options.why: Ordering by position doesn't help to find where a pattern's characters occur.

options.text: A hash set of every substring of the text
options.why: There are about n²/2 substrings, so building it is quadratic in time and space.

options.text: A suffix array (or suffix tree) built once over the text
options.why: Every occurrence of P is a prefix of some suffix, so a sorted-suffix search finds them all.

explanation: A suffix array lists the starting positions of all suffixes in sorted order. The occurrences of P form a contiguous block of suffixes that start with P, so two binary searches find it in O(m log n). A suffix tree answers the same query in O(m + occurrences). Both are built once and reused, so repeated queries never rescan the text.
reference: Gusfield, Algorithms on Strings, Trees and Sequences

stem: A Fenwick tree holds the array `[3, 2, -1, 6, 5, 4, -3, 3]` (positions 1 to 8). You add 2 to position 4, then query the prefix sum of positions 1 to 6. What is the result?

options.text: 19, the prefix sum before the update was applied
options.why: The update raises position 4 from 6 to 8, adding 2 to every prefix that includes it.

options.text: 18, the sum of positions 1 to 5 after the update
options.why: Position 6 (value 4) belongs in a prefix of length 6.

options.text: 24, the total of all eight positions after the update
options.why: Positions 7 and 8 lie outside a prefix of length 6.

explanation: A Fenwick tree answers prefix sums in O(log n): querying index 6 sums tree[6] (positions 5 and 6) and tree[4] (positions 1 to 4), since 6 − (6 & −6) = 4 and 4 − 4 = 0. The update at position 4 had already added 2 to tree[4] and tree[8]. The result matches the direct sum 3 + 2 − 1 + 8 + 5 + 4 = 21.
reference: Fenwick, "A New Data Structure for Cumulative Frequency Tables" (1994)

stem: If n distinct keys are inserted into an empty plain BST in a uniformly random order, the expected height of the tree is O(log n).

options.text: True
options.why: The expected height of a randomly built BST is about 4.311 ln n.

options.text: False
options.why: Only adversarial orders such as sorted input make a plain BST degenerate.

explanation: Random insertion order makes each key equally likely to be the root, much as quicksort picks a random pivot, so the expected depth is logarithmic. The worst case is still O(n), so code facing adversarial or sorted input needs a self-balancing tree, or a randomised structure such as a treap.
reference: CLRS, Section 12.4: Randomly built binary search trees

options.text: O(m)
O(log n)

prompts.text: Inserting a word of length m into a trie
Searching an AVL tree holding n keys
Building a segment tree over n values bottom-up
A balance check that recomputes subtree heights at every node of an n-node chain

explanation: A trie insert follows or creates one node per character. An AVL tree's height is O(log n), so search is too. Building a segment tree computes each of its about 2n nodes once. A balance check that recomputes heights at every node sums n−1 + n−2 + … on a chain, which is quadratic; computing height and balance in one pass makes it O(n).
reference: CLRS, Chapters 12 and 13; cp-algorithms: Segment Tree

stem: You insert 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 25 in that order into an empty AVL tree. Put the keys in the order a level-order traversal of the final tree visits them.
explanation: The rotations are: left at 10 (after inserting 30), left at 30 (after 50), and right-left at 20 (after 25). The final tree is 30 at the root, 20 with children 10 and 25 on the left, and 40 with a right child 50 on the right. Level order reads 30, 20, 40, 10, 25, 50.
reference: Weiss, Data Structures and Algorithm Analysis, Section 4.4: AVL trees
